analysis.one_liner: Bans most child farm labor under 14 and imposes harsher penalties for child labor violations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from its March 2022 introduction until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The CARE Act would have amended federal child labor law, which currently lets children work in agriculture at younger ages, longer hours, and more hazardous conditions than in any other industry. It would have barred employment of children under 14, ended a waiver for hand-harvest crews, banned workers under 18 from handling pesticides, required employers to report serious injuries and deaths of child farmworkers within five days, and raised penalties up to $60,115 plus possible prison time for violations that kill or seriously injure a child. It was referred to committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Child farmworkers, most of them in low-income and immigrant families, would gain higher minimum ages for farm work, a ban on handling pesticides, mandatory injury reporting by employers, and much larger financial and criminal penalties when employers break child labor law. Families would also benefit from an annual public accounting of injuries and deaths of working children.

how_it_helps.text: Revises the definition of oppressive child labor to prohibit the employment of children under 14 years of age, ending agriculture's exception that lets younger children legally work.

Raises civil penalties for child labor violations to a floor of $500 per child and up to $60,115 per violation causing serious injury, serious illness, or death of a worker under 18, doubled for repeated or willful violations.
Creates new criminal penalties of up to 5 years imprisonment for employers who repeatedly or willfully violate child labor rules in ways that cause a child worker's death or serious injury.
Requires employers to report work-related serious injuries, illnesses, and deaths of agricultural employees under 18 to the Labor Department within 5 days, with fines for failing to report.

Directs the Labor Department to revise regulations to prohibit anyone under 18 from working as a pesticide handler, and to collect and annually report data on children working in agriculture and their injuries.
Repeals the waiver provision that allowed children to be hired for hand harvesting of crops.

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers — crop growers and farm labor contractors — who rely on underage and low-cost child labor would bear higher labor costs, new injury-reporting duties, and larger fines. Some costs could pass through to food prices, and some low-income farm families would lose children's earnings opportunities on non-family farms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Crop growers and farm labor contractors

drawbacks.text: Growers would face real costs: higher wages for adult replacement workers, new injury-reporting paperwork, and fines of up to $60,115 per violation, which small farms say could be hard to absorb and could raise produce prices.

Families that rely on teens' earnings from farm work, and older children who want legal work, would lose income opportunities that current law allows; the bill preserves the parental family-farm exception but removes it for larger commercial operations.

The bill's own findings note that existing federal protections for farmworkers are seldom enforced, so the new rules would depend on enforcement capacity the government has historically not devoted to agriculture.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For children in commercial agriculture the benefits are concrete: today they can work at ages, in hours, and under hazards no other industry allows, and child farmworkers die on the job at over four times the rate of other young workers, according to the bill's own findings. The costs fall on growers and farm labor contractors in the form of higher labor costs and compliance burdens, which is precisely the behavior the penalties target. The main weakness is that penalties only matter if enforced, and the record of enforcement in agriculture is poor; but the bill's reporting and data requirements are designed partly to make enforcement possible at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on March 31, 2022, and the committee never held a markup or vote, so it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard introduced the CARE Act of 2022 in the House on March 31, 2022, with 21 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced.
Forty-seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers came out ahead: they avoided new minimum ages, the pesticide-handler ban, mandatory injury reporting, and fines of up to $60,115 per violation. Child farmworkers gained nothing, and remained eligible to work in agriculture at younger ages and under more hazardous conditions than children in any other industry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agricultural employers, who avoided new penalties

for.name: Lucille Roybal-Allard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CARE Act of 2022 and led its case that child farmworkers need the same protections other working children have.

for.name: 47 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bobby Scott, D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on March 31, 2022 — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 supporters — the sponsor plus 47 cosponsors — were House Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where the split could be measured.

industries.industry: Fruit and vegetable growers and farm labor contractors
industries.note: The bill would have raised their minimum hiring ages, ended the hand-harvest waiver, banned pesticide handling by anyone under 18, and imposed fines up to $60,115 per violation causing serious injury or death. Their interest in keeping cheap, underage labor legal ran directly against the safety of the children the bill protects.
The bill would have barred workers under 18 from pesticide handler tasks, narrowing the labor pool for hazardous chemical work and tightening the rules that govern exposure.
